passage: Vishal, you've told me three times today that you're bad at maths. Who told you that? Listen to your Rajni dadi. When I was eight, our teacher called me "the slow one". Every day: "Rajni, the slow one, try not to hold us up." So I stopped putting my hand up. Why try, if I was slow? My cousin Gopal was "the clever one". He got the hard sums, and he tried them, and he got better. Then in Class 5 a new teacher came. She gave me a hard sum and said, "You can do this. I've seen you think." I sat with it for an hour. I did it. I wasn't slow, beta. I'd just been told so often that I'd started acting it.

qa.q: What did the first teacher call young Rajni?
qa.a: "The slow one."

qa.q: Why did young Rajni stop putting her hand up?
qa.a: Being called slow every day made her believe it, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What might Vishal choose to do the next time a maths problem feels hard?
qa.a: Vishal could sit with it for a while, as young Rajni did in Class 5, instead of deciding in advance to be bad at maths.

qa.q: How might Gopal's schooling have been shaped by being called "the clever one"?
qa.a: Gopal was given hard sums and expected to try them, so he kept getting better, partly because of that label.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how being called slow made her try less while a cousin called clever took on hard work, until a new teacher believed in her.

passage: The inter-class quiz had ten minutes left, the fan was broken, and the hall was so noisy that Naveen and Suraj had to shout to hear each other. Sir dropped the last and hardest question card on their table. "Naveen, you're my clever boy, you take this one. Suraj, try not to be lazy for once, just hold the pen." Naveen grabbed the card and started working, chewing his lip. Suraj slumped back. He'd heard "lazy" so many times this year that he'd stopped doing homework at all. Why bother? "Suraj, what's seven eights?" Naveen hissed. "Fifty-six," Suraj said at once, surprised at himself. "See? You know stuff," Naveen said. Suraj sat up a little, just a little, and picked up the pen properly.

qa.q: What did Sir tell Suraj to do?
qa.a: "Try not to be lazy for once, just hold the pen."

qa.q: Why had Suraj stopped doing homework at all?
qa.a: He felt discouraged after being called lazy so many times, and had started to believe trying was pointless.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that pulled Suraj back in, and what could Sir learn from it?
qa.a: Naveen asked Suraj a real question and said "You know stuff"; Sir could try giving Suraj a real part instead of a label.

qa.q: How might Naveen be affected by always being called the "clever boy"?
qa.a: It makes him grab hard questions confidently, though it may also put pressure on him to always get them right.

grounding: In a noisy, rushed quiz, a child labelled lazy has stopped trying while his friend labelled clever takes on the hardest question.

passage: In the Andheri flat, the twins had names for everything, and so did the grown-ups. Madhav was "our little scientist". Darshan, nine minutes younger, was "the lazy one", said with a laugh at every family dinner. So when the school science fair came, Madhav signed up for the hardest project, a water filter, and worked on it every evening. Darshan said, "I'll just do a poster," and didn't finish that either. "Typical," Papa said. But Kusum maasi, visiting for the week, noticed something: Darshan fixing the broken doorbell with a screwdriver, carefully, for an hour. "That's not lazy," she told him. "That's an engineer." Darshan stared at her. The next evening he asked Madhav if he could help with the filter's pipes.

qa.q: What did Darshan fix with a screwdriver?
qa.a: The broken doorbell.

qa.q: Why might Darshan have said "I'll just do a poster"?
qa.a: After being called the lazy one at every dinner, he may have felt discouraged and believed hard projects weren't meant for him.

qa.q: Which choice by Kusum maasi changed things for Darshan?
qa.a: She noticed his careful work on the doorbell and named it, "That's an engineer", giving him a new label to live up to.

qa.q: How might Madhav's "little scientist" label have shaped his choices?
qa.a: It gave Madhav the confidence to pick the hardest project and keep at it every evening.

grounding: A child called lazy at home gives up on hard tasks while his twin, called a scientist, takes them on, until an aunt sees him differently.

passage:
"Jomon, sums done?"
"No, Ammachi. I'm slow, na. Kishore chettan does them fast."
"Try the first one."
"Why? Everyone says I'm slow. Even Miss."
"Kishore, help your brother."
"Ammachi, I'm doing the Olympiad paper. The hard one. Miss says I'm her clever boy."
"See? He gets the hard ones," Jomon said, and put his pencil down. "I get the easy ones and I still get them wrong."
"Who untangled the whole kite string yesterday? Two hours, all by himself?"
"...Me."
"Slow boys can't do that."
Jomon looked at the first sum for a long time. Then he picked up the pencil again.

qa.q: What was Kishore working on instead of helping?
qa.a: The Olympiad paper, the hard one.

qa.q: Why did Jomon put his pencil down?
qa.a: He believed the 'slow' label everyone used, so trying felt pointless next to his clever brother.

qa.q: What did Ammachi do that helped Jomon pick the pencil up again?
qa.a: She reminded him that he untangled the kite string for two hours by himself, giving him real evidence against the 'slow' label.

qa.q: How has the 'clever boy' label shaped Kishore differently?
qa.a: Being called clever makes Kishore reach for the hard Olympiad paper, while Jomon, called slow, gives up; the labels are steering both boys.

grounding: A boy repeatedly called slow stops trying while his brother, called clever, takes on hard work, until a grandmother points to evidence against the label.

passage: Last year, in Class 5, the dance teacher always called me "Lazy Kavitha", because I came late once. After that, whenever the steps got hard, I thought, why try, I'm the lazy one anyway. I stood at the back and moved slowly. Then, in the new term, Mehak Miss came. On the first day she said, "Kavitha, you have good balance. Can you try the spin at the front?" Nobody had said I had anything good. I practised the spin in our corridor every night. I fell a lot. At the annual day, I did it in the front row. I still think about how one word made me slow, and another made me try.

qa.q: What did the dance teacher call Kavitha?
qa.a: "Lazy Kavitha".

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel whenever the steps got hard?
qa.a: Kavitha felt discouraged and thought, 'why try, I'm the lazy one anyway', because the label had become part of how Kavitha saw things.

qa.q: What choice did Kavitha make after Mehak Miss's words, and what came of it?
qa.a: Kavitha practised the spin in the corridor every night, falling a lot, and finally did it in the front row at the annual day.

qa.q: How might Mehak Miss have seen Kavitha on that first day?
qa.a: Mehak Miss saw good balance, not a lazy child, perhaps because the old label had never reached the new teacher.

grounding: A child labelled lazy starts trying less, and a new teacher's belief leads the child to take on a hard spin.

passage: When I was nine, everyone at home called me "slow Rekha." Slow to eat, slow to dress, slow at sums. My cousin Noor, who lived with us, was "clever Noor." When a hard puzzle came in the newspaper, Papa gave it to Noor. When a guest asked a question, they looked at her. After a while, I stopped trying the hard sums at all. Why bother? I was the slow one. I'd just wait for Noor. And Noor, being called clever, tried everything, even things she didn't know yet. In class six, a new teacher gave me a hard problem and said, "I think you can do this." I stared at it for twenty minutes and got it right. I remember my hands shaking. I'm Rekha, and I sometimes wonder how many years that label cost me.

qa.q: How long did Rekha stare at the teacher's problem?
qa.a: Rekha stared at it for twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when solving the new teacher's problem?
qa.a: Rekha felt shaky, surprised and proud, because someone finally believed Rekha could do it.

qa.q: What does the new teacher's approach show about labels?
qa.a: Expecting Rekha to succeed gave Rekha the push to try, showing how others' beliefs shape what children attempt.

qa.q: How might being called "clever Noor" have affected Noor?
qa.a: Noor felt confident enough to try everything, even unknown things, because the label encouraged her.

grounding: A child called slow stops trying while a cousin called clever takes on hard tasks, until a teacher's belief shows how labels shape behaviour.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Tuesday.
Mridul (class four) has been called "the lazy one" by several teachers since class two, and he now says it about himself: "I'm lazy, ma'am, I won't finish." Today he didn't even start the maths worksheet. Payal, who is often called "the clever one," asked for an extra hard sheet. Both children seem to be living up to what they've heard. I sat with Mridul and asked him to do only the first three sums with me. He did them correctly and quickly. I told him, "That wasn't lazy. That was careful and fast." He looked surprised. I've asked the other teachers to stop using the word "lazy" and I'll give Mridul short challenges each day this week.

qa.q: What does Mridul now say about himself?
qa.a: He says, "I'm lazy, ma'am, I won't finish."

qa.q: How did Mridul seem to feel when the teacher called him careful and fast?
qa.a: Mridul seemed surprised and perhaps a little proud, hearing something different from his usual label.

qa.q: Why are short daily challenges and dropping the word "lazy" good steps?
qa.a: They give Mridul chances to succeed and stop reinforcing a label he has started to live up to.

qa.q: How might being called "the clever one" affect Payal?
qa.a: Payal seems encouraged to take on harder tasks, confident because others expect success.

grounding: A teacher notices a child labelled lazy tries less while one labelled clever seeks hard tasks, and works to change the label's effect.

passage:
Wednesday
At the family lunch today Bua said again, "Jasleen is the lazy one, Charu is the smart one." Everyone laughed. Charu got the hard crossword to do after lunch. I got to clear the plates.
Honestly I don't even try in maths anymore. Why? Everyone already thinks I'm lazy. If I try and fail, I'm lazy AND stupid.
Charu tries everything. Even when she gets it wrong, everyone says "good try, clever girl."
But today when I was helping Dadi with her phone, I fixed the settings in two minutes. She said, "You're so quick!" I felt warm all over.
Maybe I'm not lazy. Maybe I just stopped trying because they told me I was.
Tomorrow I'll do the maths homework properly. Just to see.
- Jasleen

qa.q: What did Bua call Charu?
qa.a: Bua said Charu is the smart one.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel when Dadi said "You're so quick!"?
qa.a: Jasleen felt warm and pleased, surprised to be praised after always being called lazy.

qa.q: What could help Jasleen break free from the label?
qa.a: Trying the maths homework properly, as Jasleen plans, and having adults notice effort, could help Jasleen see beyond the label.

qa.q: How might being called the smart one affect Charu?
qa.a: Charu seems to try everything confidently because others expect her to succeed.

grounding: A child labelled lazy by family stops trying while a cousin called smart takes on challenges, until a moment of praise makes the child question the label.

passage:
In the village school near Champhai, the teacher called Lalremsiami "slowpoke" because she took longer with sums. Soon the other children said it too.
By the end of the term, Lalremsiami stopped raising her hand. When a hard sum came, she didn't even try. "I'm slow anyway," she said.
Usha, her classmate, was called "our little genius." Usha tried every hard sum on the board, even when she got it wrong.
One day a new teacher came. She watched Lalremsiami working quietly in the back and said, "You check your answers carefully. That's a strength."
The next day, Lalremsiami raised her hand. Just once, but she did.

qa.q: What did the teacher call Lalremsiami?
qa.a: The teacher called her "slowpoke."

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami stop trying hard sums?
qa.a: Being called slow again and again made her feel small and hopeless, so she started to believe it and gave up trying.

qa.q: What did the new teacher do that helped?
qa.a: She named a real strength, careful checking, which gave Lalremsiami a new picture of herself and the courage to raise her hand.

qa.q: How does being called "our little genius" affect Usha?
qa.a: Usha feels confident and brave, taking on hard sums even when she gets them wrong.

grounding: Shows a child repeatedly called slow starting to try less, while a child called clever takes on hard tasks, and a new label changing things.

passage:
In a Cape Town primary school, Thabo was known as "the lazy one." His teacher said it when he forgot homework. His aunt said it when he didn't make his bed.
Lucia sat next to him. Everyone called her "the clever one." When the teacher asked who wanted to try the hardest puzzle, Lucia's hand went up every time.
Thabo's never did. "Lazy people don't do puzzles," he muttered.
One day the teacher gave him the puzzle anyway. He solved it in five minutes. Lucia stared. "You're good at this!"
Thabo shrugged, but he kept the puzzle sheet folded in his pocket all afternoon.

qa.q: What was Thabo known as?
qa.a: He was known as "the lazy one."

qa.q: Why did Thabo mutter "Lazy people don't do puzzles"?
qa.a: He had started to believe the label, so he felt discouraged and didn't even try.

qa.q: What could the teacher do to help Thabo more?
qa.a: Give him challenges and name his strengths, instead of calling him lazy, so he can see himself differently.

qa.q: What is it like for Lucia to be called "the clever one"?
qa.a: Lucia feels confident and keeps raising her hand for hard puzzles, as the label pushes her to try.

grounding: Shows a child called lazy starting to act the part while a child called clever takes on hard tasks, until a challenge shows a different picture.

passage:
In Class 5, the teacher sorted children into "fast" and "slow" reading groups. Jahnavi was put in "slow" after one bad reading test. Zubin was put in "fast."
By December, Jahnavi read only the easy books. When asked to read aloud, she mumbled. At home she told her mother, "I'm in slow group. I can't read big books."
Zubin, meanwhile, read chapter books and asked for harder ones. He'd started to believe he was a reader.
In January, a new librarian gave Jahnavi a book about space. Jahnavi read it in three days, hiding it under her desk.
The librarian saw and smiled. "That's a big book."
Jahnavi looked surprised. "I didn't notice."

qa.q: Which reading group was Jahnavi put in?
qa.a: She was put in the "slow" group.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi say she can't read big books?
qa.a: The "slow" label made her feel less capable, so she stopped trying harder books.

qa.q: What could the teacher change about the reading groups?
qa.a: Avoid labels like "slow" and "fast," check progress often and move children as they grow.

qa.q: How does being in the "fast" group affect Zubin?
qa.a: Zubin feels confident, sees himself as a reader and asks for harder books.

grounding: Shows a child labelled slow reading less while a child labelled fast takes on harder books, and a new book showing the slow label was wrong.

passage: Before: In the winter term, Jatin's teacher said, "Jatin, lazy again?" when he forgot his homework. The class laughed. By January, everyone called him Lazy Jatin. He stopped raising his hand. Why try? During: In February, a new teacher, Miss Elizabeth, came. On her second day, she watched him fix the broken window latch. "You're a careful thinker, Jatin. Can you help with the science model?" Jatin blinked. After: Two weeks later, Jatin stayed back after class to finish the model's wiring. Nobody called him lazy while he did it. Miss Elizabeth kept giving him harder jobs, and he kept taking them.

qa.q: What did Jatin fix on Miss Elizabeth's second day?
qa.a: The broken window latch.

qa.q: What does Jatin's "Why try?" suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt discouraged and hopeless, believing the label "lazy" was simply who he was.

qa.q: What did Miss Elizabeth do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed something he did well, called him a careful thinker, and gave him a real task, then harder ones.

qa.q: How might Jatin's classmates see him after the science model?
qa.a: They might start seeing him as capable rather than lazy, once they watch him staying back to finish the wiring.

grounding: Illustrates a child called lazy who stops trying, then takes on harder work when a teacher sees him as capable.

passage: Gurpreet, puttar, sit. You're sad because your cousin calls you slow? Listen to your Vikas Dadu. When I was ten, every Baisakhi at the fair, my uncles would laugh, "This one's a slow bullock, always last." After a while I believed them. At school I didn't even try the sums; why try if you're slow? Then a new master came. He saw me measure the wheat sacks for my father without a mistake. "Vikas, you have a sharp head. Try this." He gave me the hardest sum on the board. I got it on the third try. After that I wanted the hard ones. Words people say about you can become a coat you wear, puttar. You can take it off.

qa.q: What did Vikas's uncles call him at the Baisakhi fair?
qa.a: "A slow bullock, always last."

qa.q: How did the label make young Vikas feel?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and small, coming to believe he was slow and stopping even trying the sums.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed Vikas?
qa.a: The new master saw him measure the wheat sacks without a mistake, called him sharp and gave him the hardest sum, which he solved.

qa.q: How might the new master have felt watching Vikas solve the sum?
qa.a: He probably felt pleased and proud, seeing his belief in Vikas confirmed.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how, as a boy, being called slow made him try less and being called sharp made him take on hard tasks.

passage: The wedding house was full of noise and May heat, and the aunties kept the children busy with puzzles. "Shalini, you're the clever one, you do the big one," said Bua, handing her a five-hundred-piece jungle puzzle. "Disha, you're a bit slow, take this small one." Disha looked at her puzzle of a cat, only forty pieces. Shalini sat down happily with the jungle, frowning in concentration. Disha fitted a few cat pieces, then pushed the rest aside and wandered off to watch the dhol players. "See, she never finishes," Bua said. Nobody noticed that Disha had been the one who finished the hardest crossword at breakfast. She had just stopped trying things people said were too hard for her.

qa.q: How many pieces did the cat puzzle have?
qa.a: Only forty pieces.

qa.q: Why did Disha push the cat puzzle aside?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and hurt at being called slow, so she stopped trying and wandered off.

qa.q: What could Bua do differently next time?
qa.a: She could let both girls choose their puzzle and avoid labels like "clever" or "slow".

qa.q: How might Shalini be affected by being called the clever one?
qa.a: Shalini feels confident enough to take on the big puzzle, showing how the label pushes her to try hard tasks.

grounding: Illustrates how being called slow makes a child try less while a child called clever takes on hard tasks.

passage: All through the Delhi winter, Sonali's tuition teacher said the same thing: "Slow as a tortoise, this one." He said it whenever she took long over sums. Next to her sat Tenzin, whom he called "our little genius". By January the difference showed. When the teacher wrote a hard puzzle on the board "for extra marks", Tenzin's hand shot up; he tried it three different ways, got it wrong twice and kept going. Sonali didn't even copy it down. What was the point? Tortoises didn't get extra marks. In the auto on the way home through the fog, her mother asked how tuition went. "I'm slow," Sonali said, as if it were her name. Her mother turned round. "Who says?" Sonali shrugged and looked out at the fog.

qa.q: What did the tuition teacher call Tenzin?
qa.a: "Our little genius."

qa.q: Why didn't Sonali even copy down the hard puzzle?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and hopeless, having come to believe the "slow" label, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What could Sonali's mother do next?
qa.a: She could talk gently with Sonali about what she is good at, ask the teacher to stop using the label, and praise her effort on hard problems.

qa.q: How does being called "our little genius" affect Tenzin?
qa.a: It gives Tenzin the confidence to attempt hard puzzles and keep going after getting them wrong twice.

grounding: A child repeatedly called slow stops trying while a classmate called clever takes on hard puzzles, each living up to the label.
